3.2.2.4-f106.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Odes 3.6.23–4, the verb 'meditatur … ungui' is singular and is said of the 'matura virgo'. The sidenote does give book 5.

3.2.2.4-f113.accuracy_reason: Nepos's Lives were once attributed to Aemilius Probus, and his Epaminondas 2 records training in music and dance.

3.2.2.4-f117.accuracy_reason: This is Ovid, Met. 1.515–17, Apollo to Daphne. Patara was his Lycian oracle seat, and Burton's English leaves it out.

3.2.2.4-f126.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.4.23–4, reads 'claudere lustrum', and a lustrum is five years.

3.2.2.4-f127.accuracy_reason: Heroides 2.63–4 reads 'non est operosa … gloria', so as printed the line has lost the negative.

3.2.2.4-f128.accuracy_reason: This is Aeneid 4.93–4, Juno's sarcasm to Venus about her and her boy.

3.2.2.4-f130.accuracy_reason: Catullus 64.146–148, from Ariadne's lament. The standard text does read 'promittere parcunt' and 'dicta nihil meminere'.

3.2.2.4-f131.accuracy_reason: It is right that Tibullus (3.6, i.e. Lygdamus) and Ovid (Ars 1.633) give the laughter to Jupiter. But 'Burton gives it to Venus' overstates things: his next clause has Jupiter smile too. Tibullus 1.4 already links perjuries with Venus, so this is not simply Burton changing the god.

3.2.2.4-f133.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.277–278: 'plurimus auro / venit honos, auro conciliatur amor'. Burton does run the two clauses together.

3.2.2.4-f153.accuracy_reason: Burton's sidenote confirms that the lines come from Politian's Latin version of Moschus' 'Love the Runaway', in which Venus describes Cupid.

3.2.2.4-f167.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Pro Murena 13: 'nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit'.

3.2.2.4-f188.accuracy_reason: Jerome, Against Jovinian 1.49, quotes this from the Sentences of Sextus ('adulter est in suam uxorem amator ardentior').

3.2.2.4-f190.accuracy_reason: The closed seasons for solemnizing marriage did include Advent and Lent, among others.

3.2.2.4-f197.accuracy_reason: Apuleius, Metamorphoses 2.5, describing Pamphile. The standard text is quoted correctly.

3.2.2.4-f20.accuracy_reason: Johann Boemus wrote Omnium gentium mores. Burton's English does expand the Latin phrase.

3.2.2.4-f203.accuracy_reason: This is Metamorphoses 2.10, Lucius and Fotis, so Burton's 'lib. 11' is a mistake. 'caepi' is a spelling of 'coepi'.

3.2.2.4-f204.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Eclogue 2.21 reads 'mille meae… agnae'. The note describes the sidenote accurately.

3.2.2.4-f30.accuracy_reason: The lines are Theocritus, Idyll 8.82–83. Helen's praise is in Idyll 18. Burton does render 'os' as 'face' and calls Daphnis 'Daphne'.

3.2.2.4-f33.accuracy_reason: The note says the Latin is a version of Leucippe's rose song in Achilles Tatius 2.1. But that song is prose praise in different terms. These Latin lines (rose as flower of the gods, ornament of the Graces, kiss or darling of Dione) look like a Latin rendering of an Anacreontic rose poem, as Burton's 'out of old Anacreon belike' suggests. The glosses on 'suavium' and Burton's free English are fine.

3.2.2.4-f37.accuracy_reason: Catullus 86 ends 'omnibus una omnis surripuit Veneres' and is about Lesbia. 'Veneres' as 'charms' is correct.

3.2.2.4-f43.accuracy_reason: The Suetonian Vita Horati reads 'speculato cubiculo scorta dicitur habuisse disposita'. The note reports it correctly and rightly says Burton's version turns this into arranged mirrors.

3.2.2.4-f45.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 1.13.15–16 reads 'oscula, quae Venus / quinta parte sui nectaris imbuit'. The noun and the relative pronoun are indeed missing from Burton's line.

3.2.2.4-f48.accuracy_reason: 'Hoc non deficit incipitque semper' is the last line of the Petronian fragment 'Foeda est in coitu et brevis voluptas', which prefers kissing to intercourse.

3.2.2.4-f52.accuracy_reason: Fotis is the maidservant in Apuleius' Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), and 'pressulum' is a rare form. The sentence does go on in Burton's 'obtorto valgiter labello'.

3.2.2.4-f54.accuracy_reason: Aulus Gellius 19.11 preserves 'Dum semiulco savio / meum puellum savior…' as a Latin version of a Platonic epigram. The beloved there is a boy.

3.2.2.4-f56.accuracy_reason: In Satyricon 79 the passage runs on 'valete, curae / mortales'.

3.2.2.4-f6.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.169–70 reads 'ille dies primus leti primusque malorum / causa fuit', which refers to the meeting in the cave. The word order really is swapped in Burton.

3.2.2.4-f86.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.38 is Anna speaking to Dido. In Satyricon 112 it is the maid who quotes it to the widow, not the soldier as Burton's text implies.

3.2.2.4-f9.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Amores 2.4.32, and Burton's sidenote does say 'eleg. 2'. The glosses on Hippolytus and Priapus are correct.

3.2.2.4-f91.accuracy_reason: The sidenote cites Caspar Barth's Latin version of Aretino, the Pornodidascalus. The title belongs to the made-up Spanish count, announced by the servant whom the courtesan has disguised.

3.2.2.4-f92.accuracy_reason: Terence, Andria 555 (III.iii) reads 'amantium irae amoris integratiost'. The proverb form with 'redintegratio' is the later version.
